roles.name: Robotics, autonomy and edge AI
roles.titles: Robotics ML engineer, autonomy engineer, perception engineer, edge AI engineer, embedded ML engineer
roles.what: You make a learned model work on a machine that moves: train it, shrink it, run it inside a control loop, and prove that it is fast and safe enough.
roles.brings: ROS 2, QNX and hypervisor work, SoC bring-up and AUTOSAR are what most ML candidates lack and cannot learn in a month. Your gap is the ML side, which is what the Build closes.

rounds.name: Coding
rounds.asks: Two medium problems in 45 minutes, usually arrays, graphs or trees. Some teams ask in C++.

rounds.name: ML fundamentals
rounds.asks: Backpropagation by hand, loss functions, overfitting, why a training run diverged.

rounds.name: RL and control
rounds.asks: Value and policy methods, reward design, sim-to-real, when not to use RL at all.

rounds.name: Systems
rounds.asks: ROS 2 communication and QoS, latency budgets, quantisation, running on the target board.

rounds.name: Project deep-dive
rounds.asks: One project of yours, questioned for forty minutes. They look for what you measured.

parts.label: Coding round: data structures and algorithms
Quiz: RL, ROS 2, edge deployment, parallel computing

roles.project: Stage 7: a navigation policy you trained, running as a ROS 2 node on a Raspberry Pi, with its latency measured and written up. The racing-car replay ends in the same place.

roles.name: LLM and agentic AI engineering
roles.titles: ML engineer (LLM), AI engineer, applied scientist, agent engineer
roles.what: You build products on language models: retrieval, fine-tuning, tool-using agents, and above all the evaluation that says whether any of it works.
roles.brings: You will have written a GPT, a tokenizer and LoRA yourself by Stage 5. Most applicants have only called an API, and interviewers can tell within two questions.

rounds.name: Coding
rounds.asks: Two medium problems, often strings, hashing or graphs, in Python.

rounds.name: Transformer internals
rounds.asks: Attention with every tensor shape, positional encoding, why layer normalisation, KV caching.

rounds.name: System design
rounds.asks: Design a retrieval system or an agent for a stated task: chunking, retrieval, reranking, limits, cost, latency.

rounds.name: GenAI depth
rounds.asks: KV cache and serving, quantisation, LoRA, DPO and GRPO, RAG evaluation, prompt injection: asked as 'explain' and 'what would you change'.

rounds.name: Evaluation
rounds.asks: How would you know it works? Offline sets, checking end states, regressions, human review.

rounds.name: Project deep-dive
rounds.asks: A system you built, and the experiment that changed your mind about it.

parts.label: Coding round: data structures and algorithms
ML by hand, up to attention
Quiz: transformers, RAG, agents, generative AI systems
Interview: generative AI and system design

roles.project: Stage 9: a RAG assistant over documents you know, with hybrid search, a reranker, an evaluation set that runs in CI, and its cost and latency measured. The science-exam replay is the competition version of the same skills.

roles.name: Reinforcement learning
roles.titles: Research engineer (RL), decision science engineer, controls and learning engineer
roles.what: You train agents that act: in simulators, on robots, or inside recommendation and operations systems. Much of the work is making training stable and results reproducible.
roles.brings: Real-time and control experience from embedded work. You know what a 20 ms deadline means, which most RL candidates have only read about.

rounds.name: Coding
rounds.asks: One algorithm question and one 'implement this update rule' question.

rounds.name: RL theory
rounds.asks: Bellman equations, on-policy and off-policy, the policy gradient, GAE, why PPO clips.

rounds.name: Practice
rounds.asks: A training curve that will not rise: what do you check, in what order?

rounds.name: Probability
rounds.asks: Expectations, variance, importance sampling.

rounds.name: Project deep-dive
rounds.asks: An agent you trained, with seeds, baselines and what failed.

parts.label: Coding round: data structures and algorithms
ML by hand: networks and RL

roles.project: Stage 6: PPO written by you that solves LunarLander, then the racing-car replay, with results over several seeds.

roles.name: Federated and privacy-preserving ML
roles.titles: Federated learning engineer, privacy ML engineer, research engineer (healthcare AI)
roles.what: You train models across devices or institutions that cannot share data. It is a small field, concentrated in healthcare, finance, phones and vehicles.
roles.brings: A federated testbed of your own at NITK, an industry research internship, and an embedded background for the device side. Few candidates have all three.

rounds.name: Coding
rounds.asks: Standard medium problems; sometimes 'write FedAvg' on a whiteboard.

rounds.name: FL methods
rounds.asks: FedAvg, client drift on non-IID data, FedProx, partial participation, stragglers.

rounds.name: Privacy and security
rounds.asks: What updates leak, secure aggregation, differential privacy, poisoned clients.

rounds.name: Systems
rounds.asks: Communication cost, device limits, what happens when half the clients drop out.

rounds.name: Research discussion
rounds.asks: A paper of theirs or yours. Expect to defend an experimental setup.

parts.label: Coding round: data structures and algorithms

roles.project: Stage 8: federated training across a laptop and a Raspberry Pi on your own testbed, with non-IID data, written up with a diagram and results.

roles.name: Data scientist: banking, fintech and product
roles.titles: Data scientist, product data scientist, risk data scientist, decision scientist, ML engineer (tabular)
roles.what: You turn data into decisions: SQL and analysis, experiments, and models on tables such as fraud, credit and churn, with the statistics to say how sure you are.
roles.brings: The M.Tech's probability, statistics and data science courses, a fraud model you rebuilt from a winning solution, and engineering habits many analysts lack: version control, tests and pipelines.

rounds.name: SQL
rounds.asks: Two or three queries live: joins, GROUP BY with HAVING, window functions such as ranks, running totals and LAG.

rounds.name: Statistics and probability
rounds.asks: Bayes with base rates, distributions, intervals, what a p-value means.

rounds.name: Experiments
rounds.asks: Design an A/B test: metric, unit, sample size, duration; then the pitfalls: peeking, sample ratio mismatch, many metrics.

rounds.name: ML on tables
rounds.asks: Leakage, validation, imbalanced classes, AUC against precision at a threshold, calibration.

rounds.name: Case
rounds.asks: A metric fell last week, or a feature is about to launch: what do you check, and in what order?

roles.project: The fraud replay written up as a case study: validation by time, a threshold chosen by cost, and a plan for an A/B test that would put it live.

roles.name: MLOps and ML platform
roles.titles: MLOps engineer, ML platform engineer, ML infrastructure engineer
roles.what: You build what lets other people's models reach production and stay healthy there: pipelines, deployment, monitoring, and the tooling around them.
roles.brings: CI/CD on AWS and release discipline from automotive work. That is most of this job; the ML you need is enough to know what can go wrong with a model.

rounds.name: Coding
rounds.asks: Medium problems, plus scripting and sometimes a debugging exercise.

rounds.name: ML system design
rounds.asks: Design training and serving for a stated product: data, validation, deployment, monitoring.

rounds.name: Infrastructure
rounds.asks: Containers, orchestration, CI/CD, cloud cost, rollbacks.

rounds.name: ML judgement
rounds.asks: Leakage, drift, the right metric for a rare class, when a model should not ship.

rounds.name: Incident review
rounds.asks: A failure you handled: what you saw, what you did, what you changed afterwards.

parts.label: Coding round: data structures and algorithms
ML by hand: data, metrics, classic models
Quiz: MLOps and ML system design

roles.project: The fraud replay, run as a pipeline: time-based validation, a CI check that fails when the model gets worse, and a model that is versioned.

search.title: Getting more than one offer
points: Apply in one batch. Offers can only be compared if they arrive within the same two or three weeks.
Interview first at the places you want least. The first two interviews of any search are practice whether you plan it or not.
Ask for referrals before you apply. A referred application is read by a person; many others are not.
When one offer arrives, tell the other companies and ask whether they can finish sooner. This is normal and they expect it.
Two tracks, not five. Pick the main one and a neighbour that shares most of the preparation, such as robotics with reinforcement learning.

search.title: Checking work-life balance before you accept
points: Ask the people on the team, not the recruiter: what did last week look like, and when did you last work a weekend?
Ask about on-call: is there a rota, how often is your turn, and what happens after a night call?
Ask what drives the deadlines. Teams tied to a customer's fixed production date behave very differently from teams that ship when ready. You know this from automotive.
Ask how long the people on the team have been there. A team where nobody has stayed two years is telling you something.
Get the remote or hybrid arrangement in the offer letter, not in a conversation.

search.title: What this app cannot do
points: It can make you good at the interview. It cannot get you the interview: referrals and work that people can see do that.
The readiness figures only count what you have done here. They are a floor, not a forecast, and no figure on this page is a promise about offers or pay.
